title: APT29
summary: APT29 is a long-running intrusion set that multiple government and vendor reporting streams attribute with moderate to high confidence to a Russian foreign intelligence service, commonly identified in public reporting as the SVR. Published under names including Cozy Bear, The Dukes, NOBELIUM, Midnight Blizzard, YTTRIUM, and Iron Hemlock, the aliases reflect overlapping but not identical scopes as different publishers refined their tracking. Reporting describes sustained targeting of government agencies, diplomatic and foreign-policy institutions, think tanks, healthcare and research organisations, technology and managed service providers, and, in several documented waves, supply chains where a trusted software vendor or cloud service provider becomes the means of reaching downstream victims. The geographic emphasis in reporting is North America, Europe, and multilateral diplomatic organisations, with activity also observed against organisations in Asia and the Middle East. The tradecraft emphasised in public reporting is patient and identity-centric: password spraying and credential stuffing against exposed authentication endpoints, abuse of valid accounts including service and application identities, heavy use of cloud and identity provider APIs for discovery and persistence, token and certificate theft in some described cases, and custom implant families known for long dwell and low-noise lateral movement. Reporting has repeatedly highlighted novel persistence paths added to cloud identity platforms and the use of trusted service providers for command and control, which means endpoint-centric detection alone is insufficient. Analysts have also documented the group's preference for operating within existing administrative tooling and protocols rather than deploying conspicuous malware, complicating triage for teams whose detection strategy is signature-driven. Attribution of any given intrusion is often assessed at moderate confidence, and some activity published under these aliases may involve different operators or be contested, so defenders should distinguish between the confidence in an attribution and the confidence in the observed behaviour when writing assessments and setting detection priorities.
objectives: Explain how supply-chain and managed-service-provider access changes the victim's detection perimeter and what telemetry must be collected to compensate.
Detect password spraying and credential stuffing against cloud identity providers using sign-in risk, failure distribution, and user-agent telemetry.
Analyse cloud and identity provider audit logs to identify persistence mechanisms created through APIs rather than endpoint malware.
Explain how token, certificate, and application credential theft is detected and what revocation steps limit blast radius.
Evaluate detection coverage for adversary activity that relies on legitimate administrative tooling and explain where gaps remain.
Compare public reporting on this group's cloud tradecraft and identify which observables are durable versus environment-specific.
Build a threat hunting hypothesis for trusted service provider command and control and describe the network evidence that would confirm or refute it.
Draft a confidence-qualified attribution statement that separates observed behaviour from assessed sponsorship.

beginner.definition: APT29 is a tracking name for a patient spying group. Many governments and security companies link it to Russia's foreign intelligence service. The same activity appears as Cozy Bear, The Dukes and Midnight Blizzard. The group is known for signing in with stolen accounts instead of dropping obvious malware on computers.
beginner.whyItMatters: The letters A P T mean advanced persistent threat, a well-funded attacker that waits. This group often uses real accounts and cloud services, so nothing looks broken. Endpoint tools that only look for bad files may see nothing at all. You must watch sign-in records, permission changes and application keys, because that is where the group works.
howItWorks: The group guesses common passwords across many accounts on services open to the internet.
One sign-in works, and the attacker now has a valid account and an active session.
They add their own way back in, such as a new application key or a changed setting.
They read mail and files through normal cloud interfaces, so the traffic looks routine.
Sometimes they enter through a trusted software supplier, reaching many customers at once.
They move slowly between systems, keeping noise low and staying for many months.
beginner.example: Think of a large office tower where everyone uses a badge. A stranger watches people type their codes at the door and learns one that is simple. Now he walks in with a valid badge. He does not break windows or force doors. He sits in meeting rooms, reads files and quietly makes himself a spare badge for later.
takeaways: Watch sign-in records for many failed attempts followed by one success.
Treat cloud settings, application keys and permissions as places intruders hide.
A valid account can be more dangerous than any piece of malware.
